set1.q: Which drug is used for persistent symptoms from premature junctional contractions?
opts: Procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; a beta blocker such as metoprolol treats junctional beats.
Metoprolol
Correct. If symptoms from premature junctional contractions persist, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is used if not contraindicated; reassurance of the benign rhythm is often adequate.
Adenosine
Adenosine terminates reentrant supraventricular tachycardia for seconds; persistent junctional beats are suppressed with a beta blocker.
Atropine
Atropine speeds the sinus node in unstable bradycardia; symptomatic premature junctional beats get metoprolol.

set1.q: What is the usual prognosis of inappropriate sinus tachycardia?
opts: Most need a pacemaker
Pacemakers treat slow rhythms such as symptomatic sick sinus syndrome; a benign, unexplained sinus tachycardia does not need one.
Usually benign
Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia usually has a benign prognosis, which is why it is generally left untreated once secondary causes are excluded.
High risk of sudden death
Sudden death is a concern in rhythms such as pre-excited atrial fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is usually benign.
Progressive heart failure
Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is not described as causing heart failure; its prognosis is usually benign and it is generally left untreated.

set1.q: Sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic bradycardia is treated with which?
opts: Catheter ablation
Catheter ablation treats tachycardias from a focus or pathway; it cannot correct a sinus node that fails to fire, which needs pacing.
Adenosine
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node and would deepen any pause; symptomatic sick sinus syndrome is treated with a permanent pacemaker.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. When symptoms correlate with bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome, a permanent pacemaker is placed; tachy-brady syndrome also often needs one.
Atropine as needed
Atropine is an acute rescue for unstable bradycardia, not long-term treatment; symptomatic sick sinus syndrome needs a permanent pacemaker.

set1.q: What is the first-line treatment for stable supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, where adenosine must be avoided; stable supraventricular tachycardia starts with a vagal maneuver.
A vagal maneuver
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (which may be repeated once); an unstable patient gets immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Adenosine
Adenosine is second, given if a vagal maneuver fails in stable supraventricular tachycardia, and it may be repeated once.
Synchronized cardioversion
Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.

set1.q: A slow sinus rhythm that is causing hypotension and confusion is treated first with which drug?
opts: Metoprolol
Metoprolol is a beta blocker, and beta blockers are a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; giving one would worsen the problem.
Digoxin
Digoxin is a listed drug cause of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so it would slow the heart further rather than rescue it.
Atropine
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker if it fails; chronic symptomatic disease needs a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.

set1.q: In tachy-brady syndrome, which tachyarrhythmia is most common?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients, who then need a pacemaker with a defibrillator, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
Sinus tachycardia
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation, not a sinus tachycardia.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome a tachyarrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, alternates with symptomatic bradycardia or with offset pauses when the fast rhythm stops.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter is a fast atrial rhythm, but it is not the usual tachyarrhythmia of tachy-brady syndrome; atrial fibrillation is.

set1.q: Which drug is a direct oral anticoagulant preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation?
opts: Warfarin
Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used as an alternative with a target international normalized ratio of 2 to 3; it is not a direct oral anticoagulant.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug, not an anticoagulant; the preferred agents are direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban.
Procainamide
Procainamide is an antiarrhythmic used in atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it does not prevent clots.
Apixaban
Correct. Apixaban is one of the direct oral anticoagulants preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, with dabigatran, edoxaban and rivaroxaban.

set1.q: Which therapy is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia?
opts: Repeated adenosine
Adenosine is a diagnostic tool that usually does not terminate focal atrial tachycardia, so it cannot cure it.
A permanent pacemaker
Pacemakers treat slow rhythms; an ectopic atrial focus driving a tachycardia is cured by catheter ablation.
Atropine
Atropine speeds the heart and is used for unstable bradycardia; it has no role in curing focal atrial tachycardia.
Catheter ablation
Correct. Catheter ablation of the ectopic focus is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia, in about 90%; oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers are the initial chronic therapy.

set1.q: An educated patient stops an episode of nodal reentry at home with a vagal maneuver. What is the usual advice?
opts: Start lifelong anticoagulation
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; nodal reentry carries no such requirement.
Arrange a pacemaker
A pacemaker treats symptomatic slow rhythms; nodal reentry terminated at home needs no device.
Urgent care is not usually needed
Correct. If a vagal maneuver terminates nodal reentry in a patient who has been educated, urgent medical attention is usually not required; episodes are usually well tolerated.
Go to the emergency department
An emergency visit is not needed when an educated patient has already terminated the episode with a vagal maneuver.

set1.q: Which is a recognized cause of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Surgical injury to the node
Correct. Causes of sick sinus syndrome include sinoatrial node ischemia, injury to the node from cardiac surgery, electrolyte abnormalities, medications and hypothyroidism.
Excess thyroid hormone
It is hypothyroidism that is listed as a cause of sick sinus syndrome; excess thyroid hormone speeds the sinus rate instead.
Anemia from blood loss
Anemia drives a compensatory sinus tachycardia; the listed causes of sick sinus syndrome are node ischemia or surgical injury, electrolytes, drugs and hypothyroidism.
Heavy caffeine intake
Caffeine is a trigger for atrioventricular nodal reentry and premature atrial beats; it is not a listed cause of sick sinus syndrome.

set1.q: What is the main management of multifocal atrial tachycardia?
opts: Adenosine twice
Adenosine is used in supraventricular tachycardia through the atrioventricular node; multifocal atrial tachycardia settles with treatment of the underlying illness.
Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion does not stop several independent atrial foci; treating the underlying lung disease or heart failure does.
Treat the underlying condition

Correct. Management of multifocal atrial tachycardia is treating the underlying condition, such as decompensated lung disease or heart failure; in hospital a short course of rate control may be added.
Catheter ablation
Catheter ablation is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia (about 90%); multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the cause.

set1.q: In an older adult with new symptomatic bradycardia, which review is a key first step?
opts: The medication list

Correct. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin cause sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, so the medication list is reviewed and treating the underlying cause comes first.
A family history of fainting
Family history matters for some inherited conditions, but the drug causes of bradycardia in an older adult are found on the medication list.
A test for accessory pathways
Accessory pathways cause fast reentrant rhythms in Wolff-Parkinson-White; a new slow rhythm in an older adult first prompts a medication review.
An exercise tolerance history
Conditioning explains adaptive bradycardia in athletes, but a new symptomatic bradycardia calls for a review of rate-slowing medications.

set1.q: How is inappropriate sinus tachycardia usually managed?
opts: Usually left untreated

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, beta blockers are poorly tolerated, and the prognosis is usually benign.
Lifelong beta blocker
Beta blockers are listed as not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is generally left untreated.
Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion resets reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm and is generally left untreated.
Daily oral amiodarone
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for focal atrial tachycardia; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is benign and usually left alone after causes are excluded.

set1.q: On the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score, which result is low risk that may not need anticoagulation?
opts: 0 in a man or 1 in a woman
Correct. A score of 0 for men or 1 for women is low risk and may not require anticoagulation; patients above that typically need it unless bleeding risk is high.
2 in a man or 3 in a woman
Scores of 2 in a man or 3 in a woman are above the low-risk line of 0 for men and 1 for women, so anticoagulation is typically needed.
3 in a man or 4 in a woman
These scores are well above low risk; the low-risk result is 0 in a man or 1 in a woman.
Any score under 5
Low risk is not 'any score under 5'; the low-risk result is a score of 0 for men or 1 for women.

set1.q: On standard electrocardiogram paper, how much time does one small box represent?
opts: 0.20 seconds
0.20 seconds is one large box, made of five small boxes; a single small box between the thin lines is 0.04 seconds.
0.12 seconds
0.12 seconds is three small boxes, the upper limit of a normal QRS duration; one small box on its own is 0.04 seconds.
1.00 second
One full second takes five large boxes, or 25 small boxes, at standard paper speed; a single small box represents only 0.04 seconds.
0.04 seconds
Correct. Thin lines are 1 mm apart and each small box is 0.04 seconds; five small boxes make one large box of 0.20 seconds, and 25 small boxes make one second.

set1.q: What is the definitive management of atrial flutter?
opts: Adenosine
Adenosine may briefly slow conduction but does not cure flutter; ablation is definitive.
A pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms such as sick sinus syndrome; the flutter circuit is cured by ablation.
Vagal maneuvers
Vagal maneuvers terminate nodal reentry, not the atrial circuit of flutter, which ablation treats definitively.
Ablation
Correct. Ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate-control than fibrillation.

set1.q: In sinus arrest, which rhythm may take over?
opts: Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter is a rapid atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; when the sinus node stops in sinus arrest, the backup pacemaker is junctional.
Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation is disorganized activity with no pulse, not the escape rhythm of sinus arrest; a junctional rhythm takes over.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia comes from three or more atrial foci in acutely ill lung or heart patients; it is not the escape rhythm after sinus arrest.
A junctional rhythm
Correct. In sinus arrest the sinus node does not generate an impulse, and a junctional rhythm may take over, often with inverted (retrograde) P waves or none visible.

set1.q: In sinus node exit block, what happens to the impulse?
opts: Never generated by the node
An impulse that is never generated is sinus arrest, which can let a junctional rhythm take over; in exit block the impulse forms but cannot get out.
Blocked at the atrioventricular node
Block at the atrioventricular node is atrioventricular block, a conduction problem below the atria; exit block traps the impulse at the sinus node itself.
Replaced by a ventricular focus
A ventricular focus produces wide, bizarre complexes; exit block is a failure of the sinus impulse to leave the node, leaving a pause.
Generated, but it cannot leave the node
Correct. In sinus node exit block the sinus node generates the impulse but it does not exit to the atria, so a P wave and its beat are missing; in sinus arrest the impulse is never generated.

set1.q: Besides drugs and thyroid disease, which condition is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia?
opts: Intracranial hypertension
Correct. Increased intracranial pressure is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia, together with sinus node ischemia, late-stage infection, hypothyroidism and the rate-slowing drugs.
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, along with hypoxia, shock and myocardial infarction; it does not slow the sinus node.
Pain or anxiety
Pain and anxiety cause a physiologic sinus tachycardia, the normal response to stress, rather than bradycardia.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia is listed among the pathologic causes of sinus tachycardia; the bradycardic causes include raised intracranial pressure and sinus node ischemia.

set1.q: Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated first with which?
opts: A beta blocker

Correct. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated, or ablation when they are frequent or trigger atrial fibrillation.
Adenosine
Adenosine terminates supraventricular tachycardia for seconds; it is not used to suppress premature atrial beats.
Procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; symptomatic premature atrial beats get a beta blocker.
Amiodarone
Amiodarone is used to cardiovert focal atrial tachycardia; persistent premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker.

set1.q: Before outpatient cardioversion of atrial flutter, how long is anticoagulation given?
opts: 7 days
One week is too short; elective cardioversion follows 21 days of anticoagulation.
6 months
Six months is far longer than required; the outpatient cardioversion can follow 21 days of anticoagulation.
21 days
Correct. Outpatient cardioversion of atrial flutter (and fibrillation) is done after 21 days of anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is part of flutter management.
48 hours
48 hours is not the pre-cardioversion period given; outpatient cardioversion follows 21 days of anticoagulation.

set1.q: Adenosine slows a tachycardia and reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Which drug is used?
opts: A second dose of adenosine
More adenosine blocks only the normal atrioventricular node and leaves the accessory pathway to carry the fibrillation; procainamide is used.
Intravenous atropine
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a pre-excited tachycardia, which needs procainamide.
Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium is for torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Intravenous procainamide

Correct. If Wolff-Parkinson-White is known, or slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used; adenosine and other nodal blockers leave the accessory pathway unopposed.

set1.q: How do most people with sinus bradycardia present?
opts: With neck pulsations
Neck pulsations (the frog sign) belong to atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, a fast rhythm; most sinus bradycardia is silent.
With exertional chest pain
Chest pain marks an unstable patient, which most people with sinus bradycardia are not; the usual picture is no symptoms.
Without symptoms
Correct. Most people with sinus bradycardia are asymptomatic, and an asymptomatic sinus bradycardia is not treated.
With syncope at rest
Syncope is a feature of unstable or symptomatic bradycardia, a minority; most people with sinus bradycardia have no symptoms at all.

set1.q: How do most people with focal atrial tachycardia describe it?
opts: Neck pulsations (frog sign)
Neck pulsations, the frog sign, belong to atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia; focal atrial tachycardia presents with abrupt palpitations.
Abrupt-onset palpitations
Correct. Most people with focal atrial tachycardia report abrupt-onset palpitations, and it is generally a benign arrhythmia.
Syncope during exercise
Exertional syncope in a young person raises concern for a dangerous rhythm such as pre-excited atrial fibrillation; focal atrial tachycardia gives abrupt palpitations.
Fatigue over months
A slow, months-long course is not the picture; focal atrial tachycardia is typically paroxysmal, with abrupt-onset palpitations.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is treated how?
opts: Intravenous atropine
Atropine speeds the heart and treats unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.
Intravenous rate control
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; a stable patient without it gets rate control by mouth.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for the unstable patient; a stable patient in rapid ventricular response is rate-controlled intravenously.
Immediate ablation
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the acute treatment of rapid ventricular response.

set1.q: Which rhythm describes atrial fibrillation?
opts: Irregularly irregular, no P waves
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval, usually at 110 to 160 with a narrow QRS.
Regular, with sawtooth waves
A regular rhythm with sawtooth waves is atrial flutter, an organized atrial circuit.
Irregular, three P-wave shapes
An irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes is multifocal atrial tachycardia, which still has P waves.
Regular, with hidden P waves
A regular narrow rhythm with hidden P waves is supraventricular tachycardia such as nodal reentry; atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
set1.q: What does the HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score estimate?
opts: Need for a permanent pacemaker
Pacemaker need depends on symptomatic bradycardia; HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) estimates bleeding on anticoagulation.
Major bleeding risk on anticoagulation
Correct. The HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score estimates the risk of major bleeding in a patient on anticoagulation, to weigh risk against benefit in atrial fibrillation care.
Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation
Stroke risk is estimated with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score; HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) estimates bleeding.
Chance of returning to sinus rhythm
No listed score predicts conversion to sinus rhythm; HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) estimates major bleeding risk.

set1.q: What does a premature atrial contraction look like?
opts: An early, abnormal P wave
Correct. A premature atrial contraction begins in the atria and shows an early, abnormally shaped P wave followed by a narrow QRS.
An early wide QRS, no P wave
An early, wide and bizarre QRS with no P wave is a premature ventricular contraction.
Inverted P, narrow QRS
An inverted, buried or following P wave with an early narrow QRS is a premature junctional contraction.
A sawtooth baseline
A sawtooth baseline is atrial flutter, a sustained rhythm, not a single early atrial beat.

set1.q: Which supraventricular tachycardia is irregularly irregular?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block
Atrial flutter with a fixed 2:1 block is regular, with two sawtooth waves per QRS; atrial fibrillation is the irregularly irregular one.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves; most other supraventricular tachycardias, such as nodal reentry and focal atrial tachycardia, are regular.
Focal atrial tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia comes from one ectopic focus, so it is regular, with one consistently abnormal P wave per QRS.
Nodal reentrant tachycardia
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is a regular narrow complex tachycardia with hidden P waves.

set1.q: How does atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia usually terminate?
opts: Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; nodal reentry stops with vagal maneuvers or adenosine.
Vagal maneuvers or adenosine
Correct. Nodal reentry almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is rarely required, and episodes are usually well tolerated.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in nodal reentry; it is kept for the unstable patient.
Catheter ablation
Ablation is a definitive cure for a select subset (over 95% success), not the way a single episode is terminated.

set2.q: When is catheter ablation used for premature atrial contractions?
opts: When they trigger fibrillation
Correct. Catheter ablation is used if premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation; otherwise a beta blocker or reassurance is used.
Whenever any are found
Most premature atrial contractions are benign and asymptomatic and need no treatment, let alone ablation.
When they cause no symptoms
Asymptomatic premature atrial contractions get no treatment; ablation is for frequent beats or those triggering fibrillation.
When they come with sleep
Timing with sleep is not an indication; ablation targets frequent premature atrial beats or those triggering atrial fibrillation.

set2.q: Which cardiac event is a listed cause of junctional rhythm?
opts: Hypovolemic shock
Hypovolemia and shock drive sinus tachycardia; junctional rhythm follows inferior infarction, surgery, sinus node failure or digoxin toxicity.
Untreated hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism speeds the sinus node into tachycardia; it does not let the junction take over.
Inferior myocardial infarction
Correct. Inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause of junctional rhythm, with sinus node dysfunction, the acute period after cardiac surgery and digoxin toxicity.
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is a pathologic cause of sinus tachycardia, not junctional rhythm.

set2.q: Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia depends on which structure?
opts: A damaged sinus node
A failing sinus node is sick sinus syndrome; reentrant tachycardia needs an extra connection between atria and ventricles.
An accessory pathway
Correct. Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia is seen in patients with an accessory pathway, such as Wolff-Parkinson-White; the loop uses the atrioventricular node and the pathway.
A circuit inside the node
A circuit confined to the atrioventricular node is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, which needs no accessory pathway.
Three atrial foci
Three or more atrial foci make multifocal atrial tachycardia, an irregular rhythm without a reentry loop.

set2.q: Which atrioventricular conduction ratio is most common in atrial flutter?
opts: Correct. When the atrioventricular node blocks one of every two atrial impulses, the result is 2:1 block, the most common pattern in atrial flutter.
1:1 flutter is uncommon and dangerous, with extreme hemodynamic instability and a big risk of ventricular fibrillation; 2:1 is the common ratio.
3:1 block does occur in atrial flutter, but it is not the most common conduction pattern; 2:1 is.
4:1 block slows the ventricular rate further and is seen in flutter, but the most common ratio is 2:1.

set2.q: In sinus arrhythmia, how does the heart rate change with breathing?
opts: Unchanged; only the P-wave shape varies
A changing P-wave shape with an irregular rate suggests multifocal atrial tachycardia. Sinus arrhythmia keeps uniform P waves while the rate follows breathing.
Faster on inspiration, slower on expiration
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is irregular with a pattern: the sinus rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration, while every beat keeps a normal P wave and narrow QRS.
Slower on inspiration, faster on expiration
This reverses the pattern. In sinus arrhythmia the sinus rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration.
Faster in both phases of the breath
The rate does not rise throughout the breath; it rises with inspiration and slows with expiration, which is what makes the rhythm irregular with a pattern.

set2.q: How does age relate to the risk of atrial fibrillation?
opts: Risk falls after age 65
The opposite: being elderly is a listed risk factor for atrial fibrillation, so risk rises rather than falls with age.
Age plays no part
Age matters: the elderly are among the groups in whom atrial fibrillation is commonly seen.
Older age raises the risk
Correct. Atrial fibrillation is commonly seen in the elderly, alongside hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, family history, obesity, sleep apnea and excessive alcohol.
Risk peaks in adolescence
Atrial fibrillation is listed as common in the elderly, not adolescents; its other risk factors are cardiovascular and metabolic.

set2.q: What is the prognostic meaning of multifocal atrial tachycardia?
opts: A poor prognostic sign
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a poor prognostic sign because it occurs in acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure.
A benign finding
Benign describes focal atrial tachycardia, generally a benign arrhythmia; multifocal atrial tachycardia signals serious underlying illness.
A sign of fitness
Fitness-related findings are sinus bradycardia and junctional rhythm from high vagal tone; multifocal atrial tachycardia is a poor prognostic sign.
A normal aging change
Multifocal atrial tachycardia reflects acute illness with right heart stress, not normal aging, and it carries a poor prognosis.

set2.q: Which drug is among the medication causes of sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Digoxin
Correct. The medication causes of sick sinus syndrome are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin, all of which slow the sinus node.
Atropine
Atropine speeds the sinus node by blocking vagal input; it is the first-line treatment for unstable bradycardia, not a cause of sick sinus syndrome.
An anticholinergic
Anticholinergic drugs speed the heart and cause sinus tachycardia; the drugs that cause sick sinus syndrome are beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
A beta-agonist inhaler
Beta-agonists precipitate fast rhythms such as nodal reentry; digoxin, beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are the sick sinus drugs.

set2.q: How is sinus arrhythmia best characterized?
opts: An indication for a pacemaker
Pacemakers are for symptomatic bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome or high-grade block; sinus arrhythmia is physiologic and needs no treatment.
A normal, physiologic variant
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia is normal and physiologic: a rate of 60 to 100 that speeds with inspiration and slows with expiration, with a P wave for every QRS and nothing to treat.
A sign of sinus node disease
Sinus node disease is sick sinus syndrome, with exit block, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings; sinus arrhythmia is a normal breathing-linked variation.
A precursor of atrial fibrillation
Premature atrial contractions in a diseased heart may precede atrial fibrillation; sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiologic variant with no such role.

set2.q: Besides converting the rhythm, what can adenosine show in a supraventricular tachycardia?
opts: ST segment elevation
ST segment elevation is a sign of infarction, not something adenosine is used to uncover; slowing the rate reveals whether P waves are present.
A prolonged QT interval
A prolonged QT interval is a risk for torsades de pointes; adenosine's diagnostic value in a narrow tachycardia is revealing P waves.
A bundle branch block
Adenosine is not used to show a bundle branch block; by slowing the ventricular rate it reveals the hidden P waves of a supraventricular rhythm.
Hidden P waves
Correct. Adenosine may convert supraventricular tachycardia to normal sinus rhythm, or at least slow the rate so you can see whether P waves are there.

set2.q: Continuous atrial fibrillation lasting more than 7 days but less than one year is called what?
opts: Persistent
Correct. Persistent atrial fibrillation is continuous for more than 7 days but less than one year and needs treatment; beyond one year it is long-standing persistent.
Paroxysmal
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation lasts less than one week and usually terminates without treatment.
Long-standing persistent
Long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation is continuous for more than one year; 7 days to a year is persistent.
Permanent
Permanent is defined by a joint decision to stop attempts to restore sinus rhythm, not by a duration of 7 days to a year.

set2.q: What is the first-line treatment for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia?
opts: Amiodarone
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not a drug to speed a slow heart; atropine is first line.
A permanent pacemaker
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acute, unstable patient first gets atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Atropine
Correct. Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent pacemaker.
Adenosine
Adenosine slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia; it would worsen a bradycardia.

set2.q: How is hemodynamically stable atrial flutter treated first?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; the stable patient starts with rate control.
Immediate cardioversion
Elective cardioversion is done as an outpatient after 21 days of anticoagulation, not immediately in a stable patient.
Repeated adenosine
Adenosine is used for supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; an unstable patient gets synchronized cardioversion.

set2.q: What is a delta wave?
opts: A slurred upstroke of the QRS
Correct. The delta wave is a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex, seen with a short PR interval and a widened QRS in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A notched, wide P wave
A notched or widened P wave is an atrial finding; the delta wave is a slurred start to the QRS from early ventricular activation.
An inverted T wave
An inverted T wave is a repolarization change; the delta wave is the slurred upstroke at the beginning of the QRS complex.
A sawtooth baseline
A sawtooth baseline is the flutter wave of atrial flutter; the delta wave is a slurred QRS upstroke.

set2.q: On a rhythm strip, how does atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White differ from ventricular tachycardia?
opts: Regular sawtooth at 300
Regular sawtooth activity near 300 is the atrial rate of atrial flutter; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is irregular.
Irregular, rates under 100
An irregular rhythm under 100 is controlled atrial fibrillation without pre-excitation; with an accessory pathway the rates can approach 300.
Irregular, rates near 300
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia is regular at about 150 to 200, while atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is irregular, with some rates approaching 300.
Regular, rates 150 to 200
Regular wide complexes at 150 to 200 describe ventricular tachycardia; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is irregular and can approach 300.

set2.q: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia is more common in whom?
opts: Men
Men are less often affected; atrioventricular nodal reentry is far more common in women than in men.
People with lung disease
Severe chronic lung disease is the setting of multifocal atrial tachycardia; nodal reentry favors women without heart disease.
People with heart surgery
Prior heart surgery and atrial scarring set up atrial flutter or sick sinus syndrome; nodal reentry favors women with normal hearts.
Women
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia affects women far more than men, commonly without heart disease, spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine or alcohol.

set2.q: In sick sinus syndrome, when is observation alone appropriate?
opts: The fast rhythm is ventricular
When the tachyarrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia, the patient needs a pacemaker with a defibrillator, not observation.
Symptoms do not match the bradycardia

Correct. Management confirms whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia; if they do not, observation is appropriate, and if the bradycardia is symptomatic, a permanent pacemaker is placed.
Pauses are causing fainting
Pauses that cause fainting are symptomatic bradycardia, which needs a permanent pacemaker rather than observation.
Bradycardia causes dizziness
Dizziness that tracks with bradycardia means the episodes are symptomatic, an indication for a permanent pacemaker.

set2.q: Which rhythm most often alternates with bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome?
opts: Junctional rhythm
A junctional rhythm is a slow escape rhythm that can follow sinus arrest; the fast rhythm in tachy-brady syndrome is usually atrial fibrillation.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome, the form of sick sinus syndrome in which fast and slow rhythms alternate, the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast rhythm in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the usual one.
Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; the tachyarrhythmia that usually alternates with bradycardia is atrial fibrillation.

set2.q: Which rhythm is listed among those that can exceed 200 beats per minute and cause collapse?
opts: Physiologic sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia stays at or below about 160; the rhythms that exceed 200 are the reentry tachycardias and pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation
Correct. Rates above 200 with syncope or collapse are seen in accessory pathway reentry, nodal reentry and atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (for example Wolff-Parkinson-White).
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular rhythm of acutely ill lung or heart patients and is not among the rhythms listed for rates above 200.
Focal atrial tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia is generally a benign arrhythmia with abrupt palpitations; it is not one of the rhythms listed as exceeding 200.

opts: 100 to 160 is the range of sinus tachycardia; a junctional rhythm usually runs at 40 to 60.

Correct. A junctional rhythm is regular, usually at 40 to 60 beats per minute, with a narrow QRS and P waves that are inverted, buried or after the QRS.
60 to 100 is the normal sinus rate; a junctional escape rhythm is slower, usually 40 to 60.

set2.q: Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm at what rate?
opts: 60 to 100 beats per minute
A sinus rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal sinus rhythm; bradycardia begins below 60.
Over 100 beats per minute
A sinus rate above 100 beats per minute is sinus tachycardia, the opposite problem; sinus bradycardia is under 60.
40 to 60 with inverted P waves
A rate of 40 to 60 with inverted P waves in the inferior leads describes a junctional rhythm, not sinus bradycardia, which keeps normal upright sinus P waves.
Under 60 beats per minute
Correct. Sinus bradycardia is a regular sinus rhythm under 60 beats per minute, with a uniform P wave for every QRS, a normal PR interval and a narrow QRS.

set2.q: How is a junctional rhythm generally tolerated?
opts: Poorly, with syncope
Syncope is not the usual course; a junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated at 40 to 60.
It degenerates to fibrillation
A junctional rhythm is a stable escape rhythm, not a precursor of ventricular fibrillation; it is generally well tolerated.
Always needs a pacemaker
Only junctional rhythm from high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome needs a pacemaker; it is generally well tolerated.
Well tolerated
Correct. A junctional rhythm is generally well tolerated; management depends on the cause, from no treatment in a healthy person to a pacemaker for block or sick sinus syndrome.

set2.q: If premature atrial contractions are frequent, what should be looked for?
opts: An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway is sought when there is pre-excitation (short PR and delta wave), not because premature atrial beats are frequent.
Digoxin toxicity
Digitalis toxicity is a listed cause of junctional rhythm; frequent premature atrial contractions prompt a search for structural heart disease.
A long QT interval
QT prolongation is a risk factor for torsades de pointes; frequent premature atrial beats lead to a search for structural heart disease.
Structural heart disease
Correct. If premature atrial contractions are frequent, look for underlying structural heart disease; in a diseased heart they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, fibrillation or flutter.

set2.q: In whom are the symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia more pronounced?
opts: Women more than men
Women outnumber men in atrioventricular nodal reentry, but symptom severity is linked to older age and structural heart disease, not sex.
Elderly patients or heart disease
Correct. Symptoms of supraventricular tachycardia, such as palpitations, dyspnea and chest discomfort, may be more pronounced in the elderly and in those with underlying structural heart disease.
Young, healthy athletes
Young people without heart disease tend to tolerate supraventricular tachycardia better; symptoms are more pronounced in the elderly or with structural disease.
Patients with normal hearts
A structurally normal heart tolerates the rhythm better; symptoms are worse in elderly patients and in those with structural heart disease.

set2.q: When does atrial fibrillation become a medical emergency?
opts: Severe heart failure or infarction
Correct. Medical emergencies from atrial fibrillation include severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) and atrial fibrillation in the setting of an acute myocardial infarction.
Whenever the rate exceeds 100
A rate above 100 is rapid ventricular response, which needs intravenous rate control, but it is not by itself the listed emergency.
Whenever it is newly found
New atrial fibrillation in a stable patient is managed with rate control and anticoagulation, not as an emergency.
Whenever palpitations are felt
Palpitations are a usual symptom and atrial fibrillation is usually not directly life-threatening; the emergencies are severe heart failure or acute infarction.

set2.q: In a healthy person, a junctional rhythm often reflects what?
opts: A hidden accessory pathway
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation and reentrant tachycardia, not a slow junctional rhythm.
An overactive sinus node
An overactive sinus node gives sinus tachycardia; a junctional rhythm takes over when the sinus node slows or fails.
Atrial scarring
Atrial scarring sets up atrial flutter; in healthy athletes a junctional rhythm reflects increased vagal tone.
Increased vagal tone
Correct. Junctional rhythm can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as well-conditioned athletes, and it is generally well tolerated.

set2.q: In a stable narrow complex tachycardia, which step comes before any drug?
opts: Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide is reserved for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; the first step in stable narrow complex tachycardia is a vagal maneuver.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment only when the patient is unstable; a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.
A vagal maneuver
Correct. A vagal maneuver is first line for stable supraventricular (narrow complex) tachycardia, before adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is kept for instability.
An echocardiogram
Imaging does not terminate the rhythm; in a stable narrow complex tachycardia the first step is a vagal maneuver.

set2.q: What is the management of an asymptomatic junctional rhythm in an otherwise healthy person?
opts: No treatment

Correct. Management of junctional rhythm depends on the cause: no treatment if asymptomatic in an otherwise healthy person, a permanent pacemaker for complete or high-grade block or sick sinus syndrome.
A permanent pacemaker
A permanent pacemaker is for a junctional rhythm due to complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or sick sinus syndrome, not for a healthy, asymptomatic person.
Atropine
Atropine is used for unstable symptomatic bradycardia; an asymptomatic healthy person with a junctional rhythm needs no treatment.
Catheter ablation
Ablation destroys tissue that drives a tachycardia; it has no role in a slow, well-tolerated junctional rhythm.

set2.q: Sinus tachycardia is defined by a sinus rate in which range?
opts: From 60 to 100
A sinus rate of 60 to 100 is normal sinus rhythm; sinus tachycardia starts above 100.
From 250 to 300
An atrial rate of 250 or more, approaching 300, is atrial flutter; sinus tachycardia stays between 100 and 160.
Above 100, up to 160

Correct. Sinus tachycardia is a regular sinus rhythm above 100 up to 160 beats per minute, with a P wave for every QRS; above 160 the P waves are lost and the rhythm is called supraventricular tachycardia.
Above 160
Above 160 beats per minute the P waves are hidden and the rhythm is called supraventricular tachycardia; sinus tachycardia runs from just over 100 to 160.

set2.q: Which intravenous drug treats atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White?
opts: Magnesium
Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes; pre-excited atrial fibrillation is treated with procainamide.
Procainamide

Correct. Atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White is treated with intravenous procainamide, never adenosine, because blocking the normal atrioventricular node leaves the accessory pathway unopposed.
Adenosine
Adenosine must never be used here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Atropine
Atropine speeds conduction and is used for unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster, not slower.
